faq.question: How is usage calculated?
faq.answer: Topaz Video AI charges for source duration, first rounded up to whole seconds and then to whole billing steps. The chosen model and output tier set the step length; interpolation also depends on frame rate and slow-motion factor. Even a short clip consumes at least one step. The displayed per-second rate is the step price divided by its length. Acceptance holds the measured upload duration or the maximum linked-clip duration; unused funds return after actual usage is known, and failed jobs incur no charge. Within Topaz Video AI enlargement, the presets share a rate at a given tier except `gaia_2_animation`, which has its own pricing. Higher tiers cost more. Nyx Fast is priced below Nyx, and Hyperion 1 below Hyperion 2.5. Higher interpolation frame rates and slowing factors increase the work; Aion has the highest interpolation rate.

faq.question: What happens to the audio?
faq.answer: Enhancement and ordinary frame-rate conversion keep the sound; the tested slowed clips omit it, so a slow-motion edit needs its own audio treatment.

faq.question: How do I choose the settings?
faq.answer: Use Proteus for a general enlargement trial, Nyx for grain or Apollo for retiming; specialize only after inspecting the defect in the source.

howTo.title: Prepare a short take
howTo.body: Identify whether the shot needs more pixels, cleaner texture or a change in playback speed.

howTo.title: Choose the treatment

useCases.title: Put the clip to work
useCases.body: Prepare an old phone recording or an interview excerpt for a larger edit. Pick an enlargement preset suited to the source, then check skin, hair and compression marks before using the result in the final timeline.

useCases.title: Inspect the result
useCases.body: Work on a dim interior, a blurred dance shot or a movement study with the matching tool. Keep noise treatment, HDR conversion and slow motion as deliberate choices so you can assess each result against its source.

limits.body: Enlargement can leave compressed patches visible; a higher tier does not certify recovered source detail, and the two fixed-2× presets need a dimension check.

Denoise, Deblur & HDR processes the clip at the requested resolution. Start with `nyx` for natural-looking noise treatment, or choose `deblur` for softness. Hyperion outputs HEVC (H.265), 10-bit HDR; browser previews may fail, so review the download in an HDR-capable player or editor. Other presets output H.264. The tested Hyperion 2.5 file is tagged PQ (`smpte2084`), while the Hyperion 1 sample is tagged HLG (`arib-std-b67`); check the returned file’s HDR metadata in your player or editor.

Input is read at 30 fps for frame interpolation. With `slow_motion` above `1`, duration increases and the tested output has no audio; ordinary enhancement and frame conversion without slowing retain the soundtrack.

familyContent.closing: Trim to a useful passage of 1–60 seconds and send its MP4 through `video_url`. Start with `1080p` and the default preset for the chosen tool, keeping an untouched copy for review. A higher delivery tier cannot guarantee recovery of detail missing from the recording. Watch the full clip after processing, especially hands in motion and edges against busy backgrounds. For HDR, download the file to a compatible player or editor. For slow motion, plan a separate sound edit because the tested slowed outputs contain no audio track.

data.description: The interpolation endpoint reads the source at 30 fps and builds frames for the requested output cadence. Normal-speed conversion retains audio; the tested slow-motion results extend the action and contain no soundtrack.

paramNotes.fps: Output rate: `30`, `48`, `50`, `60` (default) or `120`; higher rates create more frames and increase cost. The source is read at 30 fps.
paramNotes.preset:
- `apollo` — precise slow motion and rate conversion, default
- `apollo_fast` — quick simple movement
- `chronos` — natural real-world motion
- `chronos_fast` — quick motion processing
- `aion` — complex high-resolution extreme slow motion

Default model: `apollo`; model selection affects the interpolation rate, with Aion the most expensive.
paramNotes.resolution: Available output tiers are `720p`, `1080p` (default), `2k` and `4k`; source framing is retained, and tier combines with model, fps and slowing to set cost.
paramNotes.slow_motion: `1` (default) keeps normal duration; `2`, `4` and `8` extend it proportionally and raise the rate. Slowed test outputs omit audio; billable duration remains the source length.
paramNotes.video_url: Input must be a linked or uploaded MP4 of 1–60 seconds; duration violations are rejected before acceptance. At normal speed audio is kept, while tested slow-motion outputs have no audio.

fps.description: Output frame rate. The source is read at 30 fps. Sets the per-second rate.

preset.description: Which Topaz interpolation model generates the new frames: Apollo, Apollo Fast, Chronos, Chronos Fast or Aion. Sets the per-second rate.

resolution.description: Resolution to process and return the clip at; the aspect ratio is kept. Sets the per-second rate.

slow_motion.description: Slow-motion factor: 2 doubles the clip's length, 4 quadruples it, 1 keeps the original speed. Billing follows the source clip's length; the factor sets the per-second rate.

video_url.description: The clip to process, 1 to 60 seconds long, as an MP4 link or upload. Length and audio are kept; clips outside that range are rejected before any charge.

data.pricingNote: Interpolation rates combine model, output tier, frame rate and slowing factor. Billing uses the original clip length, never the longer slowed result: round up to whole seconds and then complete billing steps, at least one. Divide a step’s price by its length to obtain the displayed second rate. The initial reservation covers the uploaded duration or 60 source seconds for a link; any surplus is returned on completion, and failed interpolation is not charged. More output frames and stronger slowing cost more; Aion has the highest model rate.
data.readme:
## Introduction

Frame interpolation is useful when movement needs a different rhythm: a dancer held longer in an edit, a gesture studied in detail or footage converted to a smoother playback cadence. Video AI creates intervening pictures, so review moving shapes as carefully as the reported frame rate of the returned file.

## Key features & Highlights

Apollo and Chronos each have a regular and a fast option, with Aion completing the five-model range for demanding motion. Delivery rates include 30, 48, 50, 60 and 120 fps. The source is interpreted at 30 fps, which matters when its original cadence differs from the reading assumption.

Playback rate and slowing are separate controls: a higher frame rate need not lengthen the shot, while a factor of two approximately doubles its duration. The Chronos dance run produced about 9.95 seconds at 1920×1080 and 60 fps from five source seconds. That slowed file had no audio, whereas the normal-speed Apollo Fast portrait retained its soundtrack.

## Use cases

For a dance transition, extend one selected move so it can occupy a longer musical phrase. Plan the soundtrack in the edit, since the slowed result does not supply a retimed version of the original recording.

For a movement study, keep enough action before and after the moment of interest to inspect hand and body paths. Review crossings and occlusions rather than approving solely because playback appears fluid at first glance.

## Prompt guide & Pro tips

No text instruction is accepted for retiming. Begin by deciding whether the deliverable requires a new playback cadence, longer action or both; then choose the corresponding frame rate and slowing factor. Test Apollo for general conversion or Chronos on natural movement before deciding that a heavier model is warranted.

Check the full downloaded take for doubled outlines, distorted hands and changes where one object passes another. Confirm actual runtime, fps and audio-track presence before placing it on the final timeline. Cost follows the submitted duration even when the visual result is longer, while the chosen frame rate and slow-motion factor still change the rate charged for those source seconds.

examples.note: Chronos stretches the five-second dance to approximately 9.95 seconds; the tested slowed file is silent.
